title: The Stone Hound Above the Nave

passage.title: The Stone Hound Above the Nave
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
High on the timber scaffold along the north roof of Saint Jude Abbey, apprentice stonecutter Clara brushed frost from a carved hound. Six hundred years ago, stone masons had set a row of gargoyles along the eaves. Although tourists in the courtyard below thought the winged hounds were only spooky ornaments, Clara knew their true job. Each beast had a deep stone trough carved down its spine and a wide open mouth. When heavy rain or melting snow poured off the slate roof, the stone hound shot the water clear into the street so it would not seep into the soft mortar of the lower walls.

This winter, though, a hard freeze had split the hound's lower jaw cleanly in two. Warm March winds were due by week's end. Soon the thick snowbanks on the upper roof would melt into a rushing stream. If the broken spout dribbled water straight down the wall face, the damp stone blocks above the stained-glass window would crumble. The fresh block of pale limestone, shaped with a flat chisel on the ground below, was hoisted by Clara onto the high scaffold.

Master Borel climbed up the ladder and checked the broken neck joint with his steel square. He pointed out a thin dark vein running through the old stone collar. If Clara simply glued the new jaw onto the flat break with wet lime paste, the weight of the stone would be too much. The force of spring floodwater would snap it off again. Instead, she had to carve a hidden dovetail slot that was wider at the back than at the front. That way, the new piece would lock tight into the old neck by its own shape.

For three cold hours, Clara tapped her mallet with short, steady strokes. She angled the stone channel inside the hound's throat slightly downward so no puddle could linger and freeze next winter. When she slid the new jaw into the slot, the pale limestone clicked home with barely a hairline seam. She packed warm lime mortar around the joint and wrapped it in thick burlap to cure before the night chill returned.

Two days later, a warm south wind swept across the valley and turned the roof snow into a bright torrent. Standing in the courtyard below, Clara watched a clean silver arc of meltwater leap three yards out from the stone hound's new jaws. High above the dry wall and glowing glass, her hidden joint held firm, proving that honest craft protects a building long after the scaffold comes down.

tier2Words.definition: A long, narrow open channel through which water flows
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English trog (hollowed wooden or stone channel)
tier2Words.contextClue: 'Each beast had a deep stone trough carved down its spine' to carry rain and melting snow off the roof.

tier2Words.definition: To leak or trickle slowly through small pores or cracks
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English sipian (to soak or trickle slowly)
tier2Words.contextClue: The gargoyle shoots water clear into the street 'so it would not seep into the soft mortar of the lower walls.'

tier2Words.definition: A thin line or joint where two edges meet
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English seam (line formed by joining two pieces)
tier2Words.contextClue: When Clara slid the new jaw into the slot, it 'clicked home with barely a hairline seam.'

tier2Words.definition: A fast, heavy, rushing stream of water
tier2Words.contextClue: A warm south wind 'turned the roof snow into a bright torrent' that leaped from the spout.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The fresh block of pale limestone, shaped with a flat chisel on the ground below, was hoisted by Clara onto the high scaffold."

Who or what performed the action of hoisting the limestone block?

options.text: Clara, the apprentice stonecutter on the roof
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly identifies the agent after 'by' ('by Clara') in the passive construction 'was hoisted by Clara'.

options.text: The fresh block of pale limestone
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the grammatical subject/receiver of the passive verb with the person who hoisted it.

options.text: The flat chisel used on the ground below
options.diagnosticNote: Selects a tool inside the middle participial phrase ('shaped with a flat chisel') rather than the actor.

options.text: The high timber scaffold along the north roof
options.diagnosticNote: Picks the destination object of the preposition ('onto the high scaffold') instead of the actor.

questions.provingSentenceText: The fresh block of pale limestone, shaped with a flat chisel on the ground below, was hoisted by Clara onto the high scaffold.
questions.childTip: Find the passive verb 'was hoisted by.' The name right after 'by' tells you who lifted the stone!
questions.parentExplanation: This Sentence Surgery item targets Passive Voice Actor Tracking (ELAGSE5L1). The subject 'The fresh block of pale limestone' is separated from 'was hoisted by Clara' by a 9-word modifier, requiring students to trace the agent after 'by'.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 1:

"When heavy rain or melting snow poured off the slate roof, the stone hound shot the water clear into the street so it would not seep into the soft mortar of the lower walls."

What does the word seep most likely mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: Carve a decorative wing with a steel chisel
options.diagnosticNote: Borrows stone-carving details from the passage instead of defining how water enters soft mortar.

options.text: Leap three yards outward in a bright silver arc
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses what the gargoyle spout does ('shot the water clear') with what it prevents the water from doing ('seep into the soft mortar').

options.text: Soak or trickle slowly into small cracks
options.diagnosticNote: Matches the contrast with shooting water 'clear into the street' so that moisture does not soak into the soft mortar and crumble the wall.

options.text: Shine brightly through a stained-glass window
options.diagnosticNote: Uses window imagery from Paragraph 2 rather than the context of rainwater and mortar in Paragraph 1.

questions.provingSentenceText: When heavy rain or melting snow poured off the slate roof, the stone hound shot the water clear into the street so it would not seep into the soft mortar of the lower walls.
questions.childTip: Why does the gargoyle shoot water away from the building? What would water do to 'soft mortar' if it dripped down the wall?
questions.parentExplanation: Contextual vocabulary item (ELAGSE5L4). By contrasting 'shot the water clear into the street' with 'so it would not seep into the soft mortar,' students infer that 'seep' means to soak or trickle slowly into a material.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, why did Clara angle the stone channel inside the hound's throat slightly downward?

options.text: She knew that tourists in the courtyard could only see the gargoyle if its mouth pointed straight down.
options.diagnosticNote: Borrows 'tourists in the courtyard' from Paragraph 1 and misapplies it to the internal throat channel.

options.text: She wanted the rainwater to flow backward onto the slate roof tiles above the nave.
options.diagnosticNote: Reverses the direction of water flow; the spout drains water off the roof, not backward onto it.

options.text: She ran out of pale limestone and had to make the new jaw shorter than the old one.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents a material shortage not mentioned anywhere in the text.

options.text: She wanted to make sure no puddle could stay inside the spout and freeze during the next winter.
options.diagnosticNote: Directly matches the explanation in Paragraph 4: angling the channel downward prevents standing water from freezing and splitting the jaw again.

questions.provingSentenceText: She angled the stone channel inside the hound's throat slightly downward so no puddle could linger and freeze next winter.
questions.childTip: First click the sentence in Paragraph 4 that explains why Clara angled the throat channel downward.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned with focus standard ELAGSE5RL1 (Explicit & Inferential Evidence), this Click-to-Prove item requires students to locate the exact preventive design detail in Paragraph 4 that keeps ice from cracking the replacement jaw.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 1 help set up the conflict that follows in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Paragraph 1 introduces an argument between Clara and the tourists, and Paragraph 2 shows Master Borel closing the courtyard gates.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents a conflict with tourists that never happens in the passage.

options.text: Paragraph 1 explains that gargoyles drain water off the walls, showing why the cracked jaw in Paragraph 2 threatens the abbey.
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately explains how Paragraph 1 establishes the gargoyle's protective engineering role so the reader understands the stakes of the broken jaw in Paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 1 proves that medieval masons used weak stone, and Paragraph 2 shows Clara replacing every gargoyle on the roof.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme language ('every gargoyle') and ignores that the medieval stone lasted six hundred years.

options.text: Paragraph 1 describes the warm March wind melting the snow, and Paragraph 2 flashes back to the winter storm.
options.diagnosticNote: Misstates the sequence; the approaching March thaw and winter freeze are introduced in Paragraph 2.

questions.provingSentenceText: Although tourists in the courtyard below thought the winged hounds were only spooky ornaments, Clara knew their true job.
questions.childTip: Ask yourself: why do we need to know the gargoyle's 'true job' in Paragraph 1 to understand the danger in Paragraph 2?
questions.parentExplanation: Under ELAGSE5RL5 (Story Structure), Paragraph 1 overturns the misconception that gargoyles are mere ornaments and explains their drainage function, which directly establishes why a cracked jaw in Paragraph 2 endangers the wall.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the story?

options.text: Lime mortar is strong enough by itself to hold heavy limestone blocks without any carved joints.
options.diagnosticNote: Directly contradicts Paragraph 3, where Master Borel warns that lime paste alone would snap under floodwater.

options.text: Ancient buildings should replace all carved stone spouts with modern plastic drainpipes.
options.diagnosticNote: Introduces modern plastic drainpipes not mentioned anywhere in the story.

options.text: Lasting craftsmanship relies on unseen structural care that protects a work through future storms.
options.diagnosticNote: Synthesizes the gargoyle's hidden drainage role, the dovetail joint and angled throat channel, and the concluding reflection.

options.text: Apprentices should never work on high timber scaffolds during the month of March.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme language ('never') that contradicts Clara's successful repair before the March thaw.

questions.provingSentenceText: High above the dry wall and glowing glass, her hidden joint held firm, proving that honest craft protects a building long after the scaffold comes down.
questions.childTip: Look at the final sentence of Paragraph 5 to see what Clara's 'hidden joint' proves about 'honest craft.'
questions.parentExplanation: Part A of this EBSR pair tests Theme (ELAGSE5RL2). Both the gargoyle itself (an ornament that is secretly a drain) and Clara's dovetail slot show that unseen structural integrity is what makes a building endure.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the story best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "High on the timber scaffold along the north roof of Saint Jude Abbey, apprentice stonecutter Clara brushed frost from a carved hound."
options.diagnosticNote: Introduces the character and setting in Paragraph 1 without stating the theme about lasting craftsmanship.

options.text: "This winter, though, a hard freeze had split the hound's lower jaw cleanly in two."
options.diagnosticNote: Describes the initial damage in Paragraph 2 rather than the lesson about honest craft.

options.text: "Master Borel climbed up the ladder and checked the broken neck joint with his steel square."
options.diagnosticNote: Mentions the neck joint in Paragraph 3, but does not express the overarching theme.

options.text: "High above the dry wall and glowing glass, her hidden joint held firm, proving that honest craft protects a building long after the scaffold comes down."
options.diagnosticNote: Directly proves the theme in Part A by connecting the unseen dovetail joint to lasting protection.

questions.provingSentenceText: High above the dry wall and glowing glass, her hidden joint held firm, proving that honest craft protects a building long after the scaffold comes down.
questions.childTip: Pick the exact quote in Paragraph 5 that connects 'her hidden joint' to what 'honest craft' does.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned with focus standard ELAGSE5RL1, Part B requires 100% verbatim textual proof for the theme identified in Part A.
